blocks.text: 1 Project Overview
Figure 1 Sybio-Gutweaver Project Overview

Radiotherapy for abdominopelvic tumors can cause oxidative stress, mucosal injury, and intestinal barrier disruption, and clinical management remains primarily symptomatic and supportive. Sybio-Gutweaver is developing an oral live bacterial candidate formulation based on engineered Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN), targeting radiotherapy-related acute intestinal injury.

blocks.text: The candidate product is intended to use lyophilized live bacteria and gut-release capsules, integrating a DHICA-component-optimized melanin antioxidant module, a lactate barrier-support module, an Ag43-based controllable adhesion module, and dual biosafety switches. Ag43 is used to enhance short-term retention in the target intestinal segment rather than to pursue long-term colonization. The dual safety mechanisms respectively use high-lactate-triggered Qwitch self-destruction and L-arabinose-dependent hok/sok survival licensing linked to Ag43 expression, reducing the risk of persistent output in abnormal microenvironments and dissemination after leaving predefined scenarios.

2.1 Clinical Burden of Radiotherapy-Related Intestinal Injury

Large patient base： In 2022, there were approximately 4.8247 million new cases of malignant tumors in China (Han et al., 2024). A national radiotherapy industry survey showed that in 2018, mainland China had 1,463 radiotherapy units, with approximately 1.2596 million patient visits treated annually, creating sustained demand for radiotherapy supportive care (Zhang Ye et al., 2020).

blocks.text: Relatively high acute gastrointestinal toxicity：Approximately 60%–80% of patients receiving abdominal and pelvic radiotherapy may develop acute gastrointestinal toxicity, including diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, and abnormal defecation. Intestinal crypts and epithelial cells turn over rapidly and are highly sensitive to ionizing radiation; therefore, normal intestine is an important dose-limiting tissue in abdominopelvic radiotherapy.

blocks.text: Oxidative and mucosal injury：Ionizing radiation can directly damage DNA and also induce large amounts of reactive oxygen species (ROS). After rapidly proliferating intestinal crypt stem cells and epithelial cells are damaged, villus renewal becomes insufficient, and changes such as mucosal inflammation and malabsorption occur (Hauer-Jensen et al., 2014).

blocks.text: Barrier function disruption：Epithelial injury and disruption of intercellular junctions increase intestinal permeability and may promote the translocation of microorganisms and their products across the damaged barrier. Persistent inflammation further hinders barrier recovery, causing symptoms and local tissue injury to amplify each other.

blocks.text: 2.3 Bottlenecks of Existing Therapeutic Approaches
1. Radiotherapy techniques cannot completely avoid normal intestinal exposure

segments.text: Radiotherapy techniques cannot completely avoid normal intestinal exposure

blocks.text: Precision radiotherapy such as IMRT and IGRT can reduce doses to normal tissues, but abdominopelvic tumors are anatomically close to the small intestine, colon, and rectum, making exposure of normal intestine difficult to completely avoid. In NRG/RTOG 1203, IMRT reduced gastrointestinal toxicity, but 33.7% of patients still reported frequent or persistent diarrhea at the end of treatment (Klopp et al., 2018).

segments.text: Clinical intervention remains predominantly symptom control

blocks.text: Existing management includes dietary and nutritional support, fluid replacement, antidiarrheal treatment, and some mucosal protective therapies. blocks.text: A systematic review included 23 RCTs with 1,919 patients; probiotics and synbiotics were associated with reduced risk of diarrhea, with risk ratios (RRs) of 0.71 and 0.45, respectively (Bartsch et al., 2021), indicating that local biological intervention in the gut has potential. blocks.text: 3 Pain Points of Existing Protection and Intervention Solutions
3.1 Existing Radiation Protection and Medical Intervention Solutions

Ground-based radiotherapy mainly relies on precision radiotherapy to reduce normal intestinal exposure; after injury, nutritional support, fluid replacement, antidiarrheal treatment, and other symptomatic treatments are used; microecological interventions such as probiotics and synbiotics have shown some potential. Deep-space missions mainly rely on physical shielding, mission planning, and radiation monitoring. Overall, existing solutions still lack sustained, mechanistic, and controllable intervention for local intestinal injury after radiation.

blocks.text: Through in-depth communication with Researcher Di Cuixia at the Institute of Modern Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, we further recognized that radiation injury involves multiple biological processes such as reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, oxidative stress, DNA damage, and cellular dysfunction. blocks.text: In communication with Researcher Di Cuixia, we also focused on discussing the application potential of melanin in radiation protection. Combined with the team’s proposed scheme of in situ melanin synthesis by engineered bacteria, we further recognized that evaluating melanin’s protective capacity should not only focus on yield but also on its composition and antioxidant performance. Based on this idea, the team further focused its research on DHICA-enriched melanin, hoping to use its free radical scavenging and oxidative stress-alleviating potential to reduce biological damage caused by radiation. This communication also prompted us to expand subsequent evaluation indicators from simple melanin production to ROS levels, cellular damage, and related functional indicators, thereby more systematically validating its radiation protection effects.

6.1 Innovative Drug Development Path

In the initial stage of business model design, we weighed two different development paths around the technical characteristics and application scenarios of Sybio-Gutweaver. The first was the commercialization and productization route, namely converting engineered bacterial technology into functional microecological products and rapidly achieving translation through standardized manufacturing and market channels. This path has a shorter development cycle and can enter the market relatively quickly to generate commercial returns, but it relies more on cost control, channel promotion, and brand building. For an engineered bacterial system integrating antioxidant, barrier support, controllable adhesion, and biosafety modules, developing it merely as a general microecological product may make it difficult to fully reflect its technical and therapeutic value.

segments.text: If the problems exposed at CCiC cannot be solved early, they will translate into productization risks in preclinical evaluation, CMC development, and partner due diligence, mainly in the following three aspects:

blocks.text: Front-loading of product definition. Local retention determines the actual exposure window of functional molecules. If retention degree, duration, and clearance method cannot be demonstrated, subsequent efficacy differences will be difficult to distinguish as insufficient function or insufficient delivery, and it will also be difficult to form stable candidate product specifications.

blocks.text: Upgrading of commercialization evidence. The project cannot merely prove that Ag43 “increases adhesion”; it also needs to form combined evidence on adhesion, elution, cytotoxicity, expression stability, and safety exit, and link it with lyophilization recovery, acid resistance, and intestinal release results. Ge Yin and Qi Xiaoyu of Lanzhou Science and Technology Market pointed out that investors and pharmaceutical companies focus more on reproducibility, stability, safety, and manufacturability than on a single best experimental result.
